standard.title: Develop listening and performance skills
standard.description: develop listening skills and skills for singing and playing instruments
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored their speaking and singing voices through play (AC9AMUFD01) and discovered ways voice can communicate ideas. They have not yet formally practised listening skills for specific musical purposes, ensemble blending, or instrumental technique.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop listening skills for specific musical purposes and demonstrate developing skills for singing and playing instruments across a range of sound sources.

nodes.label: Listening for specific purposes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can listen to music for at least one specific purpose (e.g. to identify tempo, match pitch, follow a count-in, or stay with the group's dynamic level).
nodes.minimum_width: Listen for one specific musical purpose in a structured activity (e.g. stay silent during rests, follow a count-in, identify when the music gets louder).
nodes.typical_width: Develop listening skills across multiple specific purposes — listening to count-ins for tempo confidence, listening to blend with others when singing in a group, listening to identify dynamics or articulation and replicating them; participate in active listening activities (moving with the beat, clapping rhythmic ideas).
wider: Participate in ensemble singing with a focus on hearing whether own voice is blending with others — practise adjusting volume in response to listening
Play musical games (e.g. call-and-response) that require listening to a specific feature and replicating it — increase the complexity of the feature over time
nodes.hinge_reason: Purposeful listening is the foundation of all ensemble and performance skill development. Students who listen passively during music activities cannot develop the pitch-matching, ensemble blending and tempo-awareness skills the descriptor requires. This cascades to AC9AMU4D01 which requires manipulating elements in response to listening.

response_modes.reason: Before each listening activity, name the specific purpose: 'This time, listen for when the music changes tempo.' After the activity, ask: 'What did you notice?' Build the habit of directed listening with explicit pre-briefing and reflective debriefing.

success_criteria: Demonstrates listening for at least one specific purpose (e.g. follows a count-in, identifies a dynamic change, matches a starting pitch)
Can describe one thing they listened for and what they noticed

nodes.label: Exploring and varying sound sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how sounds from a range of sources (voice, classroom instruments, found objects, digital instruments) can be varied using elements of music.
nodes.minimum_width: Explore at least two different sound sources; demonstrate one way each can be varied (e.g. played louder/softer, faster/slower, or with a different technique).
nodes.typical_width: Explore and improvise ways to create and vary sounds across multiple source types — voice/vocalisation, classroom instruments, found/environmental objects and digital instruments; ask and answer questions such as 'Which way of playing sounds best?' and 'What is the way I want it to sound?'
wider: Compare how the same element (e.g. dynamics) is varied differently on different instruments — what techniques are used on a drum vs a xylophone vs voice?
Explore found and environmental objects as instruments — investigate the range of sounds each can produce and how elements like articulation and tone colour vary

response_modes.reason: A rich repertoire of sound source experiences builds the tonal imagination that underpins composition and performance decisions. Students who have only explored one or two instruments default to those instruments in composition; broader exploration opens up more deliberate choices.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Sound source exploration at Y1-2 is the foundation of tonal imagination — students who have explored many sound sources (found objects, digital instruments, body percussion) bring a richer sonic vocabulary to composition and performance decisions in later bands.
success_criteria: Explores at least two different sound sources
Demonstrates at least one variation of a musical element on each source explored

nodes.label: Pitch awareness and matching
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can demonstrate developing pitch awareness — attempting to match a given pitch or adjust their singing toward a target pitch.
nodes.minimum_width: Attempt to match a given pitch when singing; describe whether their attempt was close or different.
nodes.typical_width: Participate in pitch-matching activities (e.g. echo singing, call-and-response) and gradually adjust pitch to match a partner or group; use a digital tuner or other feedback tool to develop understanding of what pitch-matching means; practise pitch awareness in singing games.
wider: Use a digital tuner to see pitch visualised — sing toward a target pitch and observe the feedback
Play echo singing games across a range of intervals — practise adjusting pitch and noticing how large vs small adjustments feel and sound

response_modes.reason: Pitch matching develops through repeated, low-stakes practice with clear feedback. Students need many opportunities to try, hear the result and adjust. Consolidation here means repeated pitch-matching activities across different musical games and singing contexts, not formal assessment.

success_criteria: Attempts to match a given pitch when singing
Shows some adjustment when aware their pitch is different from the target

nodes.label: Singing and playing technique
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can demonstrate basic technique for singing songs and playing classroom instruments with developing control.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least one specific technique for singing (e.g. using singing voice, breathing) and one for a classroom instrument (e.g. holding beaters correctly, producing a clean sound).
nodes.typical_width: Practise techniques for singing songs and playing classroom instruments across a range of repertoire — using singing voice with appropriate breath support, holding and playing instruments in ways that produce clear sound, developing accuracy and control in rhythm and pitch.
wider: Focus on a specific technique improvement across several rehearsals — compare a recording from week one with week three and describe what changed
Practise a technique (e.g. beater hold) in isolation, then apply it in a group performance — reflect on whether the technique held under performance conditions

response_modes.reason: Technique at Y1-2 requires repetition to become automatic. The consolidation investment is in returning to the same technique across multiple songs and activities so that correct hold, breath or vocal placement becomes habitual rather than effortful.

success_criteria: Demonstrates at least one correct technique for singing (e.g. using singing voice, not speaking voice)
Demonstrates at least one correct technique for a classroom instrument (e.g. holding beaters in a way that produces clear sound)
